summary: Oregon's Warrior Rock Light: an 1889 frame light and bell tower on the northern tip of Sauvie Island, replaced in 1931 by a concrete tower; still active.

structures.note: Small two-story frame building with the lens lantern and fog bell on the upper floor; replaced in 1931
Sixteen-foot sandstone base; reused under the 1931 tower; under water when the river was high
Twenty-eight-foot concrete tower on the sandstone base; struck by a barge in 1969; rebuilt by the Coast Guard (year not given in the sources read)

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends). Reached by a 0.2-mile boat ride from the St. Helens marina or a three-mile hike from the north end of Sauvie Island.

events.note: Government starts condemnation proceedings for the point because the owner asked an exorbitant sum
Title to the land obtained in December 1888; construction contract awarded
Two-story frame light and bell building on a sandstone base
Fog bell moved from Cape Disappointment by way of West Point; the Daily Morning Astorian reports it rang for the first time the Friday before 1 December 1889
Lighthouse Service asks $2,000 to buy 1.61 acres with a dwelling (LighthouseFriends)
Act of 22 October 1913 appropriates $2,000 for improvement and purchase of additional land
Cold wave from 14 January to 4 February 1930; the Columbia and Willamette froze below Portland
Barge Swan collides with the steamer Davenport in the river near the light, night of 30 March 1930
Keeper DeRoy and his son search the beach and aid eleven people after the collision
Frame building replaced by a twenty-eight-foot concrete tower on the sandstone foundation
Keeper DeRoy retires on disability after a fall at the station
Barge runs into the tower on 27 May 1969; foundation damaged, light and fog bell disabled
Fog bell removed while the Coast Guard debated rebuilding; it fell into the river and cracked, and now stands at the Columbia County Historic Courthouse in St. Helens

corrections.proposed: tower, concrete, 28 ft (8.5 m), built 1931 on the 1889 sandstone base; struck by a barge in 1969 and rebuilt by the Coast Guard
corrections.why: The 1889 building was a frame structure replaced by a 28-foot concrete tower in 1931 (LighthouseFriends; the local history site says 1930s). No source read gives 1877 for this tower; the 1877 date appears only in the Wikipedia article, which is not a citable source here.
LighthouseFriends says the lighthouse is owned by the Coast Guard, and the community history site says the Coast Guard rebuilt the tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The U.S. Lighthouse Society gives 1888 as the establishment year (title and contract were 1888; the building is 1889 per LighthouseFriends). The Astoria paper shows the station's new fog bell working by late 1889. The 1889 year is the one a visitor can source.

The OpenStreetMap figure of 28.0 matches the 28-foot tower height in the sources, so it is probably feet, not metres. The 8.5 m in the record matches 28 feet. The wikidata 9.0 m is not supported by any source read.
LighthouseFriends describes a flashing white light today. The period '4s' in the record is not checked against a light list; OpenStreetMap's 'Fl 4s' drops the colour.

notes_for_editor: Printed page numbers were not read for the Board report (scan page 456 of annualreportlig02statgoog; the report year, 1897, is inferred from the volume's order and the 1897 report's sections, so check the printed report). The Commissioner's report is cited by its printed page 54 (scan page 59), which the corpus OCR index reported. The Bulletin pages are PDF pages. ACREAGE CONFLICT: LighthouseFriends gives 1.61 acres (the 1912 request); the Commissioner's 1915 report gives one and one-eighth acres bought with the dwelling. The story gives both. YEAR CONFLICTS: station established 1888 (USLHS; first lens year 1888) vs built 1889 (LighthouseFriends, Rowlett); record 'tower built 1877' (wikidata) has no support in a source read; the Wikipedia article's 1877 and 1930 dates were not cited. The tower year is 1931 by LighthouseFriends and the USLHS place record (tower_established 1931, concrete), and 'the 1930s' by warriorrock.org. The Board's 1895 repairs list names a 'Warrior Rock post light' (unexplained, not used). FOCAL HEIGHT: record 8.5 m (ENC) not checked; OSM 28.0 and wikidata 9.0 not supported. RANGE: record 5.0 nm not checked, left out. POSITION: the record's coordinates agree with LighthouseFriends' (45.84858, -122.78835); the USLHS place record's coordinates (46.4142, -123.3138) are the roster tool's name-only match and should not be used. The 1930 barge collision and the 1930 ice account are LighthouseFriends' version of the Oregonian; the Bulletin printed the ice account, but no Bulletin text was found for the barge collision. The Astoria paper's 'new fog bell' is new to Warrior Rock, not new as a casting; the bell was cast in 1855. The Coast Guard rebuilding after 1969 has no date in the sources read; the record's ownership and access come from LighthouseFriends' page, which is undated, so confirm with the Coast Guard before publishing. Access: the tower is closed and the story says not to climb it. NRHP: not checked. Names: Frank DeRoy and the keepers are named from the roster and LighthouseFriends; the DeRoys' son and Jenny DeRoy are not named in the story (family details, no keeper role). Newspapers: Chronicling America was searched for Oregon 1887-1892; one hit (the 1889 Astorian). No 1930 Oregonian text was reachable (Chronicling America coverage ends before it). FACT-CHECK 2026-10-28: The year of the post-1969 rebuilding is not given in the sources read; this sentence moved here from the story. LighthouseFriends says the Coast Guard was still debating a rebuild when the bell came down; the community site says the Coast Guard rebuilt the tower while the bell was removed. Both are stated in the story as a disagreement. The community site spells the lieutenant 'Lt Burroughs' once; the story says Broughton, as LighthouseFriends does. The community site places the rock about a kilometre south of Warrior Point; LighthouseFriends says 'at the northern tip'; the story now says 'near the northern tip'. The fog-bell hours (344, 166, 848) come from the 1897 Board report at scan 456; the fiscal period of that table was not checked, so the story says 'the Board's report for 1897'. The printed page 54 for the 1915 Commissioner's report is the corpus OCR index reading, with no '?' flag; the page image was not opened.
